title: Africa’s governments already treat the internet as protest infrastructure. Its courts have not caught up
content:
When many people gather, some states are not prosecuting people. Instead, it cuts the network

Originally published on Global Voices

Kenya Judiciary building.  Image by Wing via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

This piece is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

On a Saturday in late July 2025, Angola shut down its internet for the first time in its recorded history. Not during an election, and not during a war. People had taken to the streets to protest the rising price of fuel. At least 22 people were killed according to the authorities’ own figures; civil society monitors counted 30 dead and more than 1,500 arrested.
snippet:
When many people gather, some states are not prosecuting people. Instead, it cuts the network

title: Digital hopes, real power: From connection to collective action
content:
Understanding how the digital rights movement evolved requires a closer look at the communities that shaped it

Originally published on Global Voices

Tahrir Square, Cairo, Egypt, February 8, 2011. Photo by Mona on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0).

This article was originally published by the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) on April 30, 2026, and an edited version is republished here with permission. It is also part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Back in 2011, the term “digital rights” was still fairly new. In the decades prior, open source and hacker communities, as well as a handful of organizations, had advocated for digital freedoms. It was through the merging of disparate communities from around the world in the 2000s that digital rights came to be more clearly understood as an extension of fundamental human rights.

title: Young people are bridging the climate divide for Oceania and the Caribbean
content:
When communities are included, when solutions are discussed, understood, and locally relevant, collaboration and participation follow

Originally published on Global Voices

Maps of Oceania and the Caribbean superimposed over the image of a young person looking at a storm brewing on the horizon. Feature image created by Janine Mendes-Franco using Canva Pro elements.

By Adele Roeder, Orit Novak, Chelsea Adams and Zahiris P. Francisco

This article was originally published by Future Forward Australia on May 10, 2026. An edited version is published here with permission.

Young people are no strangers to seeing the impacts of climate change. In Australia alone, the catastrophic Black Summer bushfires of 2019–20, record-breaking floods across northern parts of the country in 2026, and most recently, the severe tropical cyclone Narelle, which badly affected three states, have all left their mark.
snippet:
When communities are included, when solutions are discussed, understood, and locally relevant, collaboration and participation follow

title: When radio finds a new digital voice: Bringing Romani language and culture online in Kosovo
content:
Language preservation and digital inclusion can go hand in hand

Originally published on Global Voices

Radio Romano Avazo. Composition via Canva Pro.

This article was produced by Durmish Aslano from Radio Romano Avazo through the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

For years, Radio Romano Avazo has been one of the few spaces where the Romani language and culture could be heard consistently in Kosovo. Broadcasting from Prizren, the community radio station has provided content for Roma audiences who often have limited access to media in their mother tongue. 

But as media consumption increasingly moves online, one question became impossible to ignore: What happens to Romani-language content when the radio broadcast ends?
snippet:
Language preservation and digital inclusion can go hand in hand

title: How Cambodia’s law on ‘freedom parks’ curtailed people’s right to protest
content:
Only one freedom park has been identified in the country

Originally published on Global Voices

Participants hold banners while security officers block them from marching in Phnom Penh during the May 1 Labor Day. Photo from Licadho. CC BY-NC 4.0

This post is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Cambodia’s Law on Peaceful Demonstration was supposed to ensure the right of citizens to organize and participate in public assemblies by designating freedom parks in every province. But since its passage in 2009, only one park has been identified, and authorities often impose prohibitions on the use of this space for protests.

As early as 2009, several human rights groups flagged some of the restrictive provisions of the law.

Only one freedom park has been identified in the country

title: The sound of resistance
content:
A collaborative piece about different forms of protest music across time and geography

Originally published on Global Voices

Image courtesy of Sydney Allen. Made via Canva Pro.

This post is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

For nearly as long as there have been governments and a ruling class, there has been music aimed at mocking them, demanding change, and airing grievances. Music can be a powerful form of resistance — particularly in anti-democratic contexts where direct action can be risky. Music offers people a way to subvert those in power, connect with others on an emotional level, and a catchy, memorable tune can spread faster than any political speech or slogan.

title: West-to-east energy, east-to-west computing: The Uyghur costs of China’s digital order
content:
Beijing calls the Uyghur region a ‘national energy and resource strategic security base’

Originally published on Global Voices

The Karamay Cloud Computing Industrial Park of the Uyghur Region. Screenshot from Xinjiang Radio and Television Station. Fair use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

On September 14, ministers and senior officials gathered behind closed doors in Urumqi, the capital of China’s Uyghur region, on the eve of the 2026 Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Digital Economy Forum. The meeting was presented as a technical and developmental exercise in which participants discussed digital infrastructure, industrial transformation, artificial intelligence, data governance, and the economic value of data. The wider forum was held under the theme “Promoting SCO Data Connectivity, Shaping the Future with AI.”

title: In Brazil’s capital, residents grow their own heat-fighting solutions
content:
Following a national pattern, Brasília concentrates green spaces in the most affluent areas

Originally published on Global Voices

Nasaré Francisca da Silva waters crops at Floresta da Nasaré, in Ceilândia, Brazil, where her agroforestry project emerged from a rubbish tip. Photo by Fabio Pozzebom/Dialogue Earth, used with permission.

This story by Lobato Felizola was originally published on Dialogue Earth’s website on July 14, 2026. It is republished here under a partnership agreement with Global Voices, with edits. It’s also part of Dialogue Earth’s work on the Community Adaptations to City Heat (CATCH) project, in partnership with Boston University.

Brasília was designed to be a green city. Tree planting was so central to planning for the Brazilian capital that it was described as a park city. This is evident in its central area, with cool, tree-lined avenues and green parks where locals enjoy walks. The city was built in just 41 months, replacing the savanna-type biome Cerrado with a gleaming new capital.
snippet:

title: Who can speak on behalf of the people? The new frontiers of protest in the Sahel
content:
Can a democracy exist without the right to disagree?

Originally published on Global Voices

Demonstrations in the Sahel: (left) Mali, (center) Niger, and (right) Burkina Faso. Screenshots via YouTube.

This post is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In the countries of the central Sahel, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger, military juntas present themselves as the voices of restored popular sovereignty. At the same time, political parties have been dissolved in all three countries, more than a thousand civil society organizations have been suspended in Burkina Faso, and labor unions are under attack in Niger. What becomes of the right to protest when those in power claim to embody the very people on whose behalf the protests are being held?
snippet:
Can a democracy exist without the right to disagree?

title: When the right to protest remains, but demonstrating comes at a price
content:
Climate activists are particularly vulnerable to arrest and persecution

Originally published on Global Voices

A climate protest in Copenhagen. Image from Flickr. CC BY-NC-ND 2.0.

This post is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Across Europe, governments are using criminal laws against climate and environmental protesters — a phenomenon that shows few signs of retreating. A comparative study published in late 2025, examining 14 countries across the Global North and South, found that criminalization forms part of a wider pattern of repression. Researchers identified not only arrests, but new anti-protest laws, the strategic use of existing laws and legal processes, surveillance, harassment, and the public vilification of activists.

title: When telcos shut down the internet, they shut down protests for the government
content:
When the streets become too dangerous, dissent often migrates online

Originally published on Global Voices

A telecom company in Niger. Image via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

This post is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Room to protest is narrowing across much of the African continent, as governments lean on arrests, curfews, and internet blackouts to blunt dissent. When the streets become too dangerous, dissent often migrates online — which is exactly where telecommunications companies enter the picture, deciding, often under government pressure, whether a phone call gets through or a message reaches its recipient. This piece looks at how that power has been used, and at the accountability telcos have too often avoided.
snippet:
When the streets become too dangerous, dissent often migrates online

title: Bye-bye, Birdie: The Calypso King of the World dies at 91
content:
Dedicating his life to calypso shaped him into a master of the genre and consummate Caribbean man

Originally published on Global Voices

Slinger Francisco, the Mighty Sparrow, Calypso King of the World. Photo by Maria Nunes, used with permission.

Around 4:00 p.m. Trinidad and Tobago time on Sunday, September 27, the announcement that calypso legend The Mighty Sparrow had prognosticated in song for decades, finally came. In a social media post, his daughter Karen shared that the undisputed Calypso King of the World (real name Slinger Francisco) died peacefully in New York after a brief illness, at the age of 91.

“He was an institution in the entertainment industry,” she continued, “well admired for his skill and finesse as a singer, songwriter and mentor; beloved by many. He was also a husband, father, grandfather, great-grandfather, life partner and friend.”
snippet:
Dedicating his life to calypso shaped him into a master of the genre and consummate Caribbean man
